study_baseline_year <- 2013L
study_latest_year   <- 2023L
subspecialties <- c(

This document provides the supplementary methods (eMethods S1–S6), supplementary
tables (eTable S1–S3 and S7–S16), and supplementary figures (eFigure S1 and
S4–S9) for the main report. All quantities derive from the corrected census-tract–vintage lineage
described in eMethods S4 and in the main-text subsection "Data Quality: The
2019–2020 Census-Vintage Correction." Reproduction scripts are in
`scripts/manuscript_catalog/` and `manuscript/R/`.

# eMethods

## eMethods S1. Cohort determination

Subspecialists were identified from American Board of Obstetrics and Gynecology
(ABOG) certification, the source of truth for subspecialty status; Centers for
Medicare & Medicaid Services specialty codes and National Provider Identifier
(NPI) taxonomy were not used to assign subspecialty, because all OB/GYN
subspecialists report a single generic specialty under those systems. Minimally
Invasive Gynecologic Surgery is treated as an ABOG focused-practice
designation; Critical Care, Complex Family Planning–adjacent, Hospice, and
Palliative certifications held by gynecologic oncologists are merged into
Gynecologic Oncology rather than dropped. Each discipline is analyzed
separately throughout; the `r n_subspec_word` disciplines serve distinct patient
populations and are never pooled into an "any subspecialist" measure.
Board-certified subspecialists were matched to the National Plan and Provider
Enumeration System by NPI to obtain practice addresses. Participant flow and
sequential exclusions are shown in main-text Figure 1.

## eMethods S1a. Cohort tracking and data-quality validation

To ensure data quality and prevent silent data corruption throughout the multi-stage cohort construction process, we implemented a comprehensive cohort tracking system with automated validation checks. The tracking system recorded physician inclusion and exclusion decisions at each stage (ABOG roster ingestion, NPI matching, subspecialty filtering, address validation, geocoding, and isochrone generation) using a dual-identifier architecture that distinguished between pre-NPI ABOG identifiers and validated National Provider Identifiers. At each stage, the system validated identifier format integrity (10-digit NPIs, ABOG_### patterns) with hard-stop errors for format mismatches, preventing incorrect database joins.

To prevent physicians from appearing in multiple mutually exclusive categories within each stage, we implemented mutual exclusivity validation with immediate pipeline termination upon detecting duplicate categorizations. For example, physicians could not simultaneously be classified as both "name parse failures" and "no match in any of `r n_npi_match_sources` data sources" in NPI matching failures, or both "general ob-gyn with active certification" and "expired subspecialty certification" in subspecialty exclusions. The validation system included an exception mechanism for legitimate dual classifications (e.g., physicians with multiple subspecialty certifications). This validation approach prioritizes early detection of data quality violations over silent corruption, with detailed error messages identifying specific physicians and categories involved in violations.

## eMethods S1b. Supplementary physician-characteristic data sources

```{r methods-medicaid-portal-vars, include=FALSE}
# States with high-confidence Medicaid enrollment sources. Kept as vectors so the
# count reported in prose is derived from the enumerated list and can never
# disagree with it.
medicaid_opendata_states <- c("New York", "California", "Illinois")
medicaid_fhir_states     <- c("Arkansas", "Vermont", "Kentucky", "Idaho", "Washington",
                              "New Jersey", "Colorado", "Maine", "Wyoming",
                              "New Hampshire", "Michigan")
medicaid_highconf_n      <- length(medicaid_opendata_states) + length(medicaid_fhir_states)
```

These supplementary sources were used only to characterize the workforce (Supplemental Table 1A) and did not enter the accessibility estimand. To characterize the obstetric-gynecologic subspecialty workforce, we linked NPPES provider data to several supplementary administrative and research databases. Physician practice volume and service patterns were obtained from the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) Medicare Part B public use files (2013–2023), which include aggregate physician-level utilization and payment data.[@CMS2023PartB] Practice size and organizational characteristics were obtained from the Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality (AHRQ) Physician Practice and Patient Representation (3P-RD) database, a national research resource that links physician identifiers to practice-level structural characteristics including physician group size (solo, small group 2–9, medium group 10–49, large group 50+) and patient demographics. The 3P-RD database aggregates data from multiple sources including NPPES, Medicare claims, and organizational surveys to characterize how physicians are organized into practice units, enabling analyses of access implications related to practice consolidation and organizational affiliation. Historical physician location and demographic information was obtained from the National Bureau of Economic Research (NBER) processed NPPES files (2007–2023), which provide cleaned longitudinal provider data with geocoded addresses.[@NBER2023] For physicians serving Medicaid populations, we obtained Medicaid enrollment data from multiple sources with varying confidence levels. For `r medicaid_highconf_n` states, we used state Open Data portals (`r paste(medicaid_opendata_states, collapse = ", ")`) or FHIR Provider Directory APIs (`r paste(medicaid_fhir_states, collapse = ", ")`) providing high-confidence enrollment status. For remaining states, we triangulated evidence from Medicaid Managed Care Organization directories and state provider search tools (medium confidence). We did not have access to CMS Transformed Medicaid Statistical Information System (T-MSIS) or similar data due to no funding. All physician-level data sources were linked using National Provider Identifier (NPI) as the unique matching key. Only deidentified, publicly available data were used in this analysis.

## eMethods S2. Address standardization and geocoding

Provider addresses were standardized to U.S. Postal Service conventions and
geocoded against U.S. Census Bureau TIGER/Line reference data with hierarchical
fallback. Records achieving only ZIP- or place-centroid precision were excluded
to prevent spatial misclassification. Full geocoding specifications are in
`manuscript/docs/SUPPLEMENTAL_METHODS_TECHNICAL_DETAILS.md` and the drive-time
specification table (eTable S2, `tables/supplementary_table_s2_drive_time.docx`).

## eMethods S3. Drive-time isochrone generation

Geographic access was measured with network-based drive-time isochrones at
30, 60, 120, and 180 minutes, generated with the Valhalla routing engine
(v3.4) on OpenStreetMap road geometry, using the automobile costing profile
under free-flow (non–traffic-adjusted) conditions so drive times are not
sensitive to time of day. A fixed 2023 road network was applied to all study
years for routing consistency. Isochrones were not clipped to state
boundaries, so residents near state lines are credited with access to nearby
subspecialists in adjacent states (avoiding edge-effect underestimation).
Coverage attenuates sharply beyond 180 minutes, which serves as a practical
upper bound. All spatial analyses used the NAD83(2011) US National Atlas Equal
Area projection (EPSG:9311) for area computation and CONUS Albers (EPSG:5070)
for centroid-based spatial-weight construction.

These thresholds align with payer access standards: Medicare Advantage plans must ensure that 90% of beneficiaries reside within specified time and distance standards of network providers, and most state Medicaid programs (89.7%) use time and distance standards, with mean thresholds near 30 minutes for urban and 45 minutes for rural specialist access.[@Ndumele2022] The 30-minute threshold approximates the median urban state standard, 60 to 90 minutes reflect common rural specialist standards, and 180 minutes captures frontier and extremely rural populations. Network-based routing was chosen over Euclidean distance because straight-line methods overestimate underserved populations (in one Michigan hospital-access study, by 76.0%: 2.26 million versus 1.28 million residents).[@Apparicio2008]

## eMethods S4. Population weighting and census-tract vintage harmonization

Female population by race/ethnicity was drawn from American Community Survey
(ACS) 5-year estimates at the census-tract level (Table B01001 and race
subtables B01001A–I). Tract population was allocated to isochrones by
area-weighted overlap (finer than all-or-nothing centroid containment).
So that population denominators reflect real demographic change over the study
period rather than holding racial and ethnic composition artificially constant,
each analysis year was assigned its own ACS 5-year denominator, using the release
centered on that year (five-year window from two years before through two years
after the analysis year) whenever the centered release was available and
boundary-compatible. Because ACS tract geography follows the final year of each
release's five-year window, and because we analyzed populations on each release's
native tract boundaries without crosswalking, interpolating, or reweighting
populations between boundary systems, two constrained exceptions to pure centering
were required. First, analysis years 2013–2019 were analyzed on 2010-Census tract
boundaries; for 2018 and 2019, the centered releases (2016–2020 and 2017–2021) are
published on 2020 boundaries, so these two years instead used the 2015–2019
release, the final ACS release published on 2010 boundaries. Second, for analysis
year 2023, the centered release (2021–2025) had not yet been published at the time
of analysis, so 2023 used the 2020–2024 release, identical to the denominator for
2022. Analysis years 2020–2023 were analyzed on 2020-Census tract boundaries; the
tract-boundary transition therefore occurs between the 2019 and 2020 analysis
years, and no accessibility estimate compares tract-level values across the
boundary transition. Beginning with the 2018–2022 release, the Census Bureau
publishes Connecticut tracts under nine planning-region county codes rather than
the eight legacy counties; because tract boundaries were unchanged by this
recoding, Connecticut tract identifiers were mapped back to their legacy-county
equivalents using a one-to-one correspondence table derived from official
TIGER/Line geometry (identifier relabeling only; no population values were
modified). A join defect that had dropped
new-2020-vintage tracts from the overlap (defaulting them to zero coverage at
all thresholds) was identified and corrected; details, the unchanged-geometry
verification, and the corrected series are in the main-text subsection "Data
Quality: The 2019–2020 Census-Vintage Correction" and in
`docs/SUPPLEMENTAL_APPENDIX_S2_TRACT_BOUNDARY_HARMONIZATION.md`.

## eMethods S5. Statistical analysis

Population-weighted access is reported with 95% confidence intervals propagated
from ACS margins of error; these reflect ACS sampling uncertainty only and do
not incorporate spatial autocorrelation or the full complex-survey design, so
they likely understate total uncertainty. Temporal trends used weighted least
squares (inverse-variance weights) with Newey-West heteroskedasticity- and
autocorrelation-consistent standard errors (lag 4, prespecified from ACS
5-year survey overlap). Demographic comparisons are reported as differences
with margins of error rather than as hypothesis tests. The ecological
tract-level logistic models (eTable S10) are reported as associations, not
individual-level effects.

For `r study_baseline_year`-versus-`r study_latest_year` comparisons, percentage-point changes were tested with z-tests using standard errors derived from ACS 90% margins of error (MOE₉₀ = 1.645 × SE); the standard error of the difference was SE_diff = √(SE₂₀₂₃² + SE₂₀₁₃²), treating the two time points as independent (a conservative assumption, since repeated tract measurements are positively correlated, yielding wider intervals and more stringent tests). Overlapping 95% confidence intervals do not preclude significance under the z-test. Prespecified race-specific contrasts (main-text Figure 3, eTable S3) used Holm-Bonferroni control of the family-wise error rate (α = 0.05) within each race/ethnicity group across the four drive-time thresholds; other subgroup analyses were exploratory and reported without multiplicity adjustment. A Durbin-Watson statistic was reported as a residual-autocorrelation diagnostic; HAC standard errors, not ordinary regression standard errors, were used for inference. Exact P values are reported to three decimals for P ≥ .001 and as P < .001 below that.

All figures use colorblind-accessible palettes (Okabe-Ito and Tableau guidelines, verified with the colorblindcheck package for deuteranopia, protanopia, and tritanopia), perceptually uniform sequential scales for maps, and were generated at 600 DPI. Analyses used `r R.version.string` (R Foundation for Statistical Computing)[@RCoreTeam2023] with tidycensus 1.7.3,[@Walker2024] sf 1.0-14,[@Pebesma2018] spdep 1.3-3, ggplot2 3.4.4, and dplyr 1.1.4; all stochastic procedures used fixed random seeds (seed = 12345).

## eMethods S6. Sensitivity analyses

Three sensitivity analyses accompany the primary ABOG-only estimand:
(i) alternative drive-time thresholds (`manuscript/R/create_supplementary_threshold_sensitivity.R`);
(ii) inclusion of urology-pathway (American Board of Urology) urogynecologists
as a cohort-definition sensitivity for the urogynecology discipline (main-text
"Sensitivity Analysis: Urology-Pathway Urogynecology"); and
(iii) discipline-exclusive and access-breadth decompositions (eTable S8-S9).

# eTables

## eTable S1. Sixty-minute access by state and discipline

Population-weighted percentage of women within a 60-minute drive of a
subspecialist in each discipline, by state (2023). Each discipline analyzed
separately; not pooled.

```{r etable-s1-per-state}
d <- stat_csv("tableS_per_state_access60.csv")
if (!is.null(d)) {
  if ("state_fips" %in% names(d) && "st" %in% names(d)) {
    d$state_fips <- NULL
    names(d)[names(d) == "st"] <- "State"
  }
  kable(d, align = c("l", rep("r", ncol(d) - 1)))
} else cat("_Pending: run scripts/manuscript_catalog/compute_comparator_additions.R_")
```

## eTable S8. Access breadth: women by number of disciplines reaching their tract

Distribution of U.S. women by how many of the `r n_subspec_word` disciplines reach their
census tract at 60 minutes (reached = majority of tract women within a
60-minute drive; 2023).

```{r etable-s8-breadth}
d <- stat_csv("tableS_access_breadth.csv")
if (!is.null(d)) {
  d$women <- round(d$women / 1e6, 1); d$pct <- round(d$pct, 1)
  names(d) <- c("Disciplines reaching tract", "Women, millions", "% of women")
  kable(d, align = c("c", "r", "r"))
} else cat("_Pending._")
```

## eTable S10. Ecological correlates of tract-level 60-minute access (full model, all terms)

Adjusted and unadjusted odds ratios (95% CI) from a separate logistic
regression per discipline; outcome = majority of tract women within 60 minutes.
Race/ethnicity terms are per 10-percentage-point increment relative to
non-Hispanic White share; `rural` = RUCA ≥4 vs urban. Ecological (tract-level)
associations.

```{r etable-s10-logistic}
d <- stat_csv("table_poor_access_logistic.csv")
if (!is.null(d)) {
  d$`Univariable OR (95% CI)` <- sprintf("%.2f (%.2f to %.2f)", d$uni_or, d$uni_lo, d$uni_hi)
  d$`Adjusted OR (95% CI)` <- sprintf("%.2f (%.2f to %.2f)", d$multi_or, d$multi_lo, d$multi_hi)
  out <- d[, c("subspecialty", "term", "n_tracts", "pct_reached",
               "Univariable OR (95% CI)", "Adjusted OR (95% CI)")]
  names(out)[1:4] <- c("Discipline", "Term", "Tracts (n)", "% reached")
  kable(out, align = c("l", "l", "r", "r", "r", "r"))
} else cat("_Pending._")
```

## eTable S15. Full deprivation-adjusted ecological models with interactions (all terms, all disciplines)

Adjusted odds ratios (95% CI) and P-values for every term of the per-discipline
logistic model (outcome = tract reached at 60 min; predictors = race/ethnicity
shares per 10 pp, rural, poverty per 10 pp, no-vehicle per 10 pp, and
rurality-by-race interactions). Tract-level ecological associations.

```{r etable-s15-interactions}
d <- stat_csv("table_interaction_models.csv")
if (!is.null(d)) {
  d$`OR (95% CI)` <- sprintf("%.2f (%.2f to %.2f)", d$or, d$lo, d$hi)
  d$P <- signif(d$p, 3)
  out <- d[, c("subspecialty","term","OR (95% CI)","P","n_tracts")]
  names(out)[c(1,2,5)] <- c("Discipline","Term","Tracts (n)")
  kable(out, align = c("l","l","r","r","r"))
} else cat("_Pending: run scripts/manuscript_catalog/compute_inferential_models.R_")
```

## eTable S16. Bootstrap disparity gaps and group access (2023)

Cross-discipline-mean 60-minute access by mutually-exclusive race-alone group,
and tract-resampling bootstrap 95% CIs (2,000 replicates) for the disparity gaps.

```{r etable-s16-bootstrap}
g <- stat_csv("table_bootstrap_group_access.csv")
b <- stat_csv("table_bootstrap_gaps.csv")
if (!is.null(g)) { names(g) <- c("Race-alone group","Access, % (cross-discipline mean)"); kable(g, align=c("l","r")) }
if (!is.null(b)) {
  b$`95% CI` <- sprintf("%.2f to %.2f", b$ci_lo, b$ci_hi)
  names(b)[1:2] <- c("Contrast","Estimate (pp)")
  kable(b[, c("Contrast","Estimate (pp)","95% CI")], align=c("l","r","r"))
} else cat("_Pending: run scripts/manuscript_catalog/compute_bootstrap_gaps.R_")
```

# eFigures

## eFigure S5. Bivariate maps: 60-minute access by minority share, all `r n_subspec_word` subspecialties

```{r efig-s5-bivariate, out.width="100%"}
p <- fig_path("figure6_bivariate_go_access.png")
if (file.exists(p)) include_graphics(p) else cat("_Pending: run build_bivariate_hotspot_map.R_")
```

One panel per discipline. Census tracts classified by a bivariate 3 by 3 scheme
crossing that discipline's 60-minute access (fixed thirds of the 0 to 100%
coverage scale) with minority population share (tertiles, held constant across
panels). Darkest cell = low access co-occurring with high minority share. Grey =
no data (Wyoming). Shared arrow legend: `figure6_bivariate_legend.png`. This
bivariate access-and-minority-share framing follows prior work linking
distance-weighted spatial access, residential segregation, and a downstream
clinical outcome (late-stage breast-cancer diagnosis).[@Dai2010]

## eFigure S6. Getis-Ord Gi* hotspots of 60-minute access, all `r n_subspec_word` subspecialties

```{r efig-s6-hotspots, out.width="100%"}
p <- fig_path("figure7_getis_ord_go_hotspots.png")
if (file.exists(p)) include_graphics(p) else cat("_Pending._")
```

One panel per discipline. Local Getis-Ord Gi* on tract-level access with
k-nearest-neighbor (k=8) spatial weights; blue = significant low-access clusters
(access deserts), red = high-access clusters. Grey = no data (Wyoming).

## eFigure S7. Illustrative coverage gain from optimally siting additional subspecialists

```{r efig-s7-optimization, out.width="90%"}
p <- fig_path("figure8_optimization_curve.png")
if (file.exists(p)) include_graphics(p) else cat("_Pending: run compute_optimization_counterfactual.R_")
```

One curve per discipline. Sixty-minute access as a function of the number of
additional subspecialists sited by a greedy maximal-coverage heuristic, in which
each candidate's catchment is approximated by a 60-km great-circle radius
(calibrated to a 60-minute drive). Illustrates the *shape* of achievable gains
and diminishing returns, not a precise siting plan.

## eFigure S8. Temporal tract-level urogynecology (FPMRS) access, 2020-2022

```{r efig-s8-fpmrs-temporal, out.width="100%"}
p <- fig_path("Figure2_FPMRS_Temporal_Access.png")
if (file.exists(p)) include_graphics(p) else cat("_Pending: run manuscript/R/create_figure_fpmrs_temporal_map.R_")
```

Faceted census-tract choropleths of the percentage of women within a 60-minute
drive of an FPMRS (urogynecology) subspecialist, by year. The panel window is
**2020-2022**, the complete years available on a single, internally consistent
tract layer. The tract-level accessibility surface is reported on the seam layer
(the lineage that produces the manuscript's headline numbers). Two exclusions
define the window: (i) the terminal study year **2023** is right-censored and
reporting is still accruing, so it is shown only as a separately-labeled
provisional panel (eFigure S9), not alongside the complete years; and (ii)
**2019** is omitted because it uses the 2010 Census-tract vintage whereas 2020
onward use the 2020 vintage, so a 2019 panel joins only ~84% of tracts to the
2020-vintage geometry (versus ~99.7% for 2020-2022) and, being pre-2020, contains
no Wyoming. Per-year cohorts mean the headline access numbers never compare
tracts across the 2019/2020 vintage break (eMethods "Data Quality: The 2019-2020
Census-Vintage Correction"), and this figure likewise stays on one vintage.
Produced by `manuscript/R/create_figure_fpmrs_temporal_map.R` (default = complete
years >= 2020; override the floor with `FPMRS_MAP_MIN_YEAR`).
